newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Congo wants own experts with UN massacre probe.
newsitem.headline: Congo wants own experts with UN massacre probe.

text.p: President Laurent Kabila's Congo said on Thursday it wanted its experts to work alongside a U.N. team probing allegations that his forces or their Tutsi allies massacred Rwandan Hutu refugees.

But Justice Minister Mwenze Kongolo said the experts could not be present when the investigators, prevented from starting on time by a dispute with Kabila's government over membership of the team, interviewed potential witnesses.
"The principle is accepted, they must do their work, but they must work with us," he told a news conference.
"We wanted our experts to be there to observe their work, but not during interviews," he said. "Our experts must be there to observe facts that will be found on the spot."

At the United Nations in New York, Foreign Minister Bizima Karaha was more conciliatory, saying that having people accompanying the U.N.team was a question of security rather than interference or observation.
"If the U.N. feels they can travel alone, we are ready to allow them to do that. If they want us to help them, we can do that also. We have a responsibility to protect them," he said.

Procedures for the investigation have become almost as controversial as the probe itself, with Kabila having rejected the head of the first Geneva-based team, Roberto Garreton of Chile, because of his report from eyewitnesses that said massacres had taken place.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan then said he would organise the investigation himself, drawing criticism from human rights groups against the United States for not having put pressure on Kabila to allow in the original team.

In Santiago, Chile, Garreton said his new report, to be released soon, would show more than 40 sites for massacres he mentioned previously during a brief visit to Zaire in March and another to Rwanda in May.
"We will keep working although we can't enter the country, by using eyewitness account and other reports," he said of his team authorised by the U.N. Commission on Human Rights.
On Thursady, Annan conferred alone with Karaha, who told reporters "we want to know the truth about what happened in our country and this investigation is an opportunity to ask and know clearly."
In answer to questions, he said his government thought Garreton "was not neutral enough."

But he said screening the new team was not a condition of the investigation. "We sincerely believe that the team which will come will come to work with us. In one way or another they will have to deal with us so the more we know them the better, but it is not a condition," he said

The Democratic Republic of the Congo, formerly Zaire, has also demanded that the probe be extended back to 1993 so as not only to cover Kabila's seven-month rebellion that toppled veteran dictator Mobutu Sese Seko in May.
"Today Roberto Garreton is no longer part of the commission. We are content that the date had been put back," Kongolo said in Kinshasa.

Over a million Hutus crossed into the former eastern Zaire fearing reprisals for the 1994 genocide in Rwanda of minority Tutsis by Hutu hardliners. The bulk returned home but relief officials say up to 200,000 remain unaccounted for.
